newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai police probe brokerages after bank rumours.
newsitem.headline: Thai police probe brokerages after bank rumours.

text.p: Police on Thursday raided at least two foreign brokerages to investigate if they were behind rumours that some medium and small Thai banks might be suspended by authorities, industry sources said.
"Police walked in and questioned our staff and executives...," said an official of ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett Asia, one of the two houses raided.
The management of Capital Nomura Securities Plc confirmed that police had visited the company to look at its telephone and fax records late last week.

"We have fully cooperated with police officers. We would like to clear this as soon as possible in order to maintain our integrity and reputation," said Vicharat Vichit-Vadakan, Capital Nomura's chief executive.
Government spokesmen last week said rumours about troubled Thai banks were spread by fax messages to other countries by some equities research houses that held malicious views on Thailand.
George Morgan, country manager for ABN AMRO Hoare Govett Asia, denied in a statement that his company had circulated a fax message that the Thai government was going to close down the banks.

"We are in fact very positive on the Thai stock market. We issued an overweight recommendation on the Thai stock market at the end of June and have been going through a significant level of business channelling foreign funds into the stock market since then," he said.
"Moreover, we are about to invest US$60 million of our own money in the Thai financial sector through acquisition of Asian Securities Trading," he added.
Officers at a special police unit set up by Deputy Interior Minister Chalerm Yubamrung to screen press reports said they were not aware of the raids.
The country is suffering its worst economic slump in more than a decade with severe problems in its financial and property sectors.
On July 2, the authorities floated the baht, which led to a de fact devaluation of between 15 and 20 percent.

Bangkok Metropolitan Bank Plc, Siam City Bank Plc, First Bangkok City Bank Plc, Laem Thong Bank Plc and Union Bank of Bangkok Plc have denied they were potential targets of suspenion by the government.
The Bank of Thailand also denied the rumours.
But the talk caused a slide in prices on the Thai stock market as investors steered clear of some banking stocks.

Former finance minister Amnuay Viravan, his adviser and former deputy central bank governor Ekamol Khiriwat, and Viroj Nualka, chairman of Phatra Thanakit Plc, on Thursday denied Thai press speculation they might have been behind the rumours against the banks.
Amnuay said in a statement the rumours were fabricated and he would take legal action against people or newspapers further suggesting that he and his advisers were behind them.
A senior police officer told reporters that the management of any companies found guilty of spreading unfounded rumours faced a maximum penalty of seven years in jail.
